title: Knee Arthritis (Osteoarthritis): Symptoms, Treatment and When Surgery Is Needed
metaDescription: Knee arthritis explained simply: symptoms, causes, whether it gets worse, treatment step by step, and when knee replacement is worth considering. Thane.
intro: Knee arthritis (osteoarthritis) means the smooth cushion in your knee has become rough and thin. It cannot be cured, but most people can reduce pain and keep moving well with medicines, exercise and simple changes, and only a small number ever need surgery. This guide answers the questions patients ask most, from "why is my knee cracking?" to "do I need a knee replacement?". It is for anyone with ghutne dard or gudghe dukhi.

sections.heading: What is knee arthritis?
sections.body: It is wear and change inside the knee joint. The smooth cushion on the ends of the bones (cartilage) becomes rough and thin, and the bone and tissues around it react. Some people grow small bony lumps, called spurs. It mostly develops slowly over many years. Doctors call it osteoarthritis.

sections.heading: What does knee arthritis feel like?
sections.body: Pain that is worse when you move or at the end of the day, and eases with rest. Stiffness after sitting that settles once you get going. You may also notice a grinding or crunching feeling, swelling, or the knee giving way. Good days and bad days are normal.

sections.heading: Why did I get it?
sections.body: There is rarely one cause. The NHS lists getting older, an earlier knee injury, being overweight, a family history, other joint diseases such as gout or rheumatoid arthritis, and being a woman as risk factors. Heavy physical work also raises the risk. Normal walking and exercise do not cause it.

sections.heading: Will it get worse?
sections.body: Not necessarily. For many people it changes very little, and for some it settles and then stays steady. For others it progresses faster. Nobody can promise which, but staying active and keeping your weight in check gives your knee a good chance.

sections.heading: How do I treat it? Our usual step-by-step approach
sections.body: We usually go one step at a time, starting with the simplest treatment, and move on only if you still have pain. The plan is always tailored to you, so some steps may be skipped or repeated.
bullets: Step 1: Medicines. Painkiller gels or tablets to settle the pain.
Step 2: Exercises. Once the pain is calmer, strengthening and walking to build the muscles around the knee.
Step 3: Physiotherapy treatments. Ultrasound, shockwave or short-wave can be added for pain relief only, if pain is still holding you back.
Step 4: Injection. A steroid injection for pain relief if the knee is still not settling.
Step 5: Surgery. A partial or total knee replacement only if your daily life is still badly affected and it suits you.

sections.heading: When is surgery the right choice?
sections.body: When knee pain keeps limiting your daily life even after the earlier steps have been given a fair trial. Surgery is not the first answer, and your X-ray alone does not decide it. If an operation makes sense, we explain the options, including partial and total knee replacement, and you decide whether to go ahead.

sections.heading: When should I see a doctor?
sections.body: See a doctor if knee pain has lasted more than a few weeks, is waking you at night, or is limiting your walking or stairs. Go the same day if the knee is suddenly hot, red and very swollen, especially with fever, if it is locked, or if you cannot put any weight on it.

faqs.a: There is no cure, but treatment can ease symptoms a lot, and it does not always get worse. Medicines, exercise and weight control are the main tools.

faqs.q: At what age does knee arthritis start?
faqs.a: It is more common after about 45, but it can start earlier, especially after a knee injury.

faqs.q: Is walking good for knee arthritis?
faqs.a: Yes, in most cases. Staying active keeps the muscles strong and the knee less stiff. Build up slowly and let pain guide you.
An X-ray can help your doctor plan treatment, but the amount of damage it shows does not reliably predict how much pain you have. There is no blood test for knee arthritis.

faqs.q: Does knee arthritis always need a knee replacement?
faqs.a: No. Most people never need surgery. It is considered only when pain still limits daily life after other treatment.

faqs.q: Can knee arthritis happen in both knees?
faqs.a: Yes, and one knee often troubles you more than the other. Each knee is treated according to its own symptoms.
